doc.title: Chazz Frichtel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 13, 2016

title: Versatility and a typical week in Los Angeles
summary: He explains the L.A. scene demands versatility; his weeks mixed private casuals, sessions, demos, prerecords and his own original band.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: I’m assuming that you have to be fairly versatile.

Yeah. Yeah. It’s amazing. The L.A. music scene is probably — because of TV and film a little bit more popular music oriented than say New York or the jazz scene in New York, although there’s a vibrant jazz scene in L.A. But yeah, you pretty much have to be able to understand a lot of different genres of music, especially if you’re going in as a studio player and have the skills needed for session work, which is being able to read and understand and decipher a chart and those kind of things, but understanding different styles of music, whether it’s rock or Latin music or film cues, things like that. So versatility is important. It’s important.

So you are predominantly a bassist and a singer, and you also are a songwriter. I’ve seen you playing guitar on the internet. All those things together, if you look at your week, a typical week now or 20 years ago, what was a typical week like for you?

Well a typical week, it all depends on what years we’re talking about. When I first got to L.A. in the late 70s, actually most of my career I’ve spent probably the most time playing the bass and singing. That’s what I got hired for and that’s what I kind of built my reputation on. But all along the way I’ve also played guitar and I play piano a little bit, enough to accompany myself. I would never book myself as a guitarist per se, but I kind of played James Taylor style, that kind of thing. But a typical week used to be generally on the weekends there’d be like private functions. One of the great things in L.A., when I first got there there was a lot of live music happening in the clubs and there was also a lot of live playing going on which in New York they call club dates and out there we call casuals. And they would be private functions in Beverly Hills or Bel Air or around town. And what was great about that was that you could wind up on a gig and all of a sudden in walks Ernie Watts or some other guys from The Tonight Show band and you’re like, “wow, that’s Ernie Watts.” And so we did that kind of work, there were lots of sessions going on, people needing tracks for their demos, we did some prerecord things for Vegas shows, it was busy. And then I was always — always had kind of an original band going so we were always in the studio cutting tracks and trying to get some kind of deal going, which eventually almost led to near-bankruptcy.
